## Phenomenon

Every orbit closure contains a closed orbit. For a reductive group acting on an affine variety, disjoint closed invariant subsets are separated by invariants [@mumford1965, Ch. 1, §2]. Since an invariant is constant on each orbit, and hence on its closure, every orbit closure then contains exactly one closed orbit. For a unipotent group acting on an affine variety, every orbit is closed [@rosenlicht1961], so every orbit closure is a single orbit. In neither case can an orbit closure contain two closed orbits.

The Borel subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is neither reductive nor unipotent. It acts linearly on $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with an orbit closure containing two closed orbits.

## Setup

- **Field and characteristic:** an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic zero. The computations below use only that the characteristic is not $2$.
- **Group:** the upper triangular Borel subgroup
$$
B=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&t\\0&a^{-1}\end{pmatrix}:a\in k^*,\ t\in k\right\}
\subset \mathrm{SL}_2 .
$$
- **Representation:** $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, with coordinates
$$
X=\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\z&-x\end{pmatrix}.
$$
- **Action:** conjugation.

## Construction

The polynomial $q=x^2+yz=-\det(X)$ is invariant. Put
$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Direct calculation gives
$$
\begin{pmatrix}a&t\\0&a^{-1}\end{pmatrix}
A
\begin{pmatrix}a&t\\0&a^{-1}\end{pmatrix}^{-1}
=\begin{pmatrix}t/a&a^2-t^2\\a^{-2}&-t/a\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Thus
$$
B\cdot A=\{x^2+yz=1,\ z\ne0\}.
$$
Indeed, given a point on the right, choose $a$ with $a^{-2}=z$ and put $t=ax$; the equation then forces $y=a^2-t^2$. Since this is a nonempty open subset of the irreducible quadric $Q=\{x^2+yz=1\}$, its closure is all of $Q$.

## Proof of the orbit decomposition

Setting $z=0$ gives $x=\pm1$, so
$$
Q\setminus(B\cdot A)=L_+\sqcup L_-,\qquad
L_\pm=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}\pm1&y\\0&\mp1\end{pmatrix}:y\in k\right\}.
$$
These are disjoint closed affine lines. Conjugation by $u(s)=\begin{pmatrix}1&s\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ sends $y$ to $y-2s$ on $L_+$ and to $y+2s$ on $L_-$. Each line is therefore a single $B$-orbit. The orbit closure $Q$ has exactly three orbits: one open orbit and two disjoint closed orbits.

## Outro

The two closed orbits $L_+$ and $L_-$ are not separated by invariants. Every invariant is constant on the orbit $B\cdot A$, hence by continuity on its closure $Q$, which contains both $L_+$ and $L_-$.

The same configuration, two distinct closed orbits in one orbit closure, occurs in the quotient stack $[\mathbb P^1/\mathbb G_m]$ [@alper2013, Example 8.4]. Here $[Q/B]\simeq[\mathbb P^1/T]$, with $T$ acting with weight $2$ on an affine coordinate; the effective action is the usual $\mathbb G_m$-action. In the present example the configuration occurs in a linear representation.

## References and related examples

Gandini describes this three-orbit decomposition on $\mathrm{SL}_2/T$ [@gandini2018, Example 3.3]. The identification with $Q$ is $gT\mapsto g\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)g^{-1}$.

Kraft, crediting tom Dieck, describes the quadric $\mathrm{SL}_2/T$ as a principal $\mathbb G_a$-bundle over the affine line with a doubled origin: the quotient by the upper unitriangular subgroup $U\subset B$ [@kraft1996, §3].
